explained.validators.hardware.meta.title: Validator hardware: what to run a 6529 validator on
explained.validators.hardware.meta.descr: Home and office tiers first, then datacenter and cloud options with instance types and prices at nine providers, your own Ethereum node, and how large TDH holders run several machines.

explained.validators.hardware.chooser.in: Up to three questions, one suggestion. Change an answer to see another. In the test phase, any machine works.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.wh: Can a computer at your home or office be on for a few hours a day?
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.no: Will you also run your own Ethereum node?
You don’t need one. The validator checks every answer it gets from any Ethereum server.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.sp: Do you already have a computer you can use for this?
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.ac: Start with the computer you have.
Any {bits} computer with a current Linux, macOS or Windows ({x64} only) runs the validator; {cores} and {ram} of memory leave room to spare. Turn off sleep, and plug in a network cable if you can.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.go: Put it on wired Ethernet, with a small battery backup (UPS). About {month} a month: its price spread over four years, plus about {watts} of power.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.gr: Run a home server with its own Ethereum node.
Your validator then reads Ethereum from a node you run. Plan on {ram} of memory, a {disk} NVMe drive that is TLC with DRAM, and a UPS.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.ra: A dedicated server with unmetered traffic runs the validator and an Ethereum node. The server priced below has {spec}. A smaller one runs a node from {small} a month; a big cloud charges {cloud}. Choose rack mode at setup and open the port you set.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.cl: Any VM with {vcpu} and {ram} of memory works; {ram8} is enough. Choose rack mode at setup and open the port you set. If you can run a machine at home or at work later, it helps the network more.
explained.validators.hardware.home.why: Why home and office come first
explained.validators.hardware.home.sprea: Homes spread the network across many people, places and internet providers.
Cloud VMs gather in a few companies’ buildings. One of the network’s goals is that no single hosting company or internet provider carries more than a third of the validators’ weight.
explained.validators.hardware.home.priva: At home, Tor keeps your address private.
The validator opens no port and sends its traffic through Tor, so peers and Ethereum servers don’t see your address. A cloud VM is tied to a billing account.
explained.validators.hardware.home.costC: A Good mini PC costs about {good} a month, power included.
explained.validators.hardware.home.cost: That is about {fourYears} over four years, hardware and power. The cheapest VM at AWS, Google Cloud or Azure costs {cloud} a month, about {cloudFourYears} over four years. A budget VPS, such as OVHcloud’s at {ovh} a month, costs about as much as the mini PC.
explained.validators.hardware.tier.accep: about {month} a month for a new Pi
explained.validators.hardware.tier.basis: Prices read {date}. New hardware costs more than it did a year ago, because memory and flash prices rose in {year}. Power at {kwh} a kWh, the US average for {month}.
explained.validators.hardware.tier.goodD: The drive a mini PC comes with, {min} or more, is enough for the validator. The tier’s {range} leaves room for other uses; a node needs a {node} drive of its own.
explained.validators.hardware.tier.terms: The validator reads Ethereum from public servers and checks every answer against Ethereum’s own block headers.
A fast SSD that plugs straight into the board.
A battery backup that keeps the machine and the router on through short power cuts.
explained.validators.hardware.dc.intro: If you can’t keep a machine at home or at work, a datacenter is a fine place for a validator. It is also a good place for a second machine. Both options run in rack mode: choose it at setup and open the port you set.
explained.validators.hardware.dc.rackCos: Rented: {spec}, enough for its own Ethereum node. Colocation: about {colo} a month, plus {server} for the server.
explained.validators.hardware.dc.cloudCo: With {ram} of memory. Data coming in is free at every provider.
explained.validators.hardware.every.wire: When it reads from public servers, about {wire} a month crosses your connection, compressed.

explained.validators.hardware.cloud.tipA: Arm types cost less at AWS and Azure, and the validator has an Arm build for Linux.
explained.validators.hardware.cloud.tipB: Burstable types are fine. The validator works a few minutes a day, so its daily average stays far below their baseline.
explained.validators.hardware.cloud.tipS: The network doesn’t yet publish which providers and countries validators run in. Until it does, keep each of your machines at a different provider, and not all in one country.
explained.validators.hardware.node.label: Your own node
explained.validators.hardware.node.title: Running your own Ethereum node
explained.validators.hardware.node.p1: You don’t need one. Any Ethereum server works, because the validator checks every answer against Ethereum’s own block headers. A server can be slow or stop answering, but it can’t make your validator sign a wrong result.
explained.validators.hardware.node.p2: A node of your own keeps your Ethereum reads private and adds a data source that no company runs. It needs far more than the validator does.
explained.validators.hardware.node.stora: {disk} of TLC NVMe with DRAM. A full node’s database is {db} today, depending on the client, and ethereum.org expects {small} to be too small by {by}. Network disks are too slow.
explained.validators.hardware.node.inter: {down} down and {up} up. 6529’s own node sent its peers about {upload} a month while it was syncing.
explained.validators.hardware.node.softw: An execution client and a consensus client. The consensus client adds {consensus} of disk.
explained.validators.hardware.node.growt: The database keeps growing. The latest published rates are from {year}, at half of today’s gas limit, so expect faster growth now.

explained.validators.hardware.holders.ti: Setting up several machines under one account
explained.validators.hardware.holders.pl: A plan that spreads the network: a Good mini PC at home, and a Rack server or Cloud VM in another country, at a provider your other machines don’t use. Read Ethereum from your own node on one and from public servers on the other, so no single data source carries your whole account.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.gr: Make a key on each machine, then list every key in one grant from your wallet, up to {keys}. Each key gets a share of your weight; give the most reliable machine the largest, for example {syntax}. The steps are in the install guide that comes with the validator, under “Several machines for one account”.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.do: While one machine is down, the others still sign their shares. Your account stays registered as long as any of its keys signs within seven days.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.ba: A backup is another key in the grant, never a copy of a key. Restoring a copied key on a day its old machine already signed is a double vote, and it excludes your whole account.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.wa: Sign the grant from a cold or hardware wallet. At home, keep Tor on and publish no location.

explained.validators.hardware.faq.label: Questions
explained.validators.hardware.faq.title: Questions operators ask
explained.validators.hardware.faq.off.q: Can I turn the machine off at night?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.off.a: Yes, if it is on for about three hours a day, any time between {open} and {close}. It signs within minutes, and at home it then waits up to two hours before it sends its vote. {open} falls in the late afternoon or evening in the Americas, after midnight in Europe and in the morning in East Asia. Your account stays registered for seven days without a signature, and this release has no penalty for being offline; the only fault is signing twice.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.node.q: Do I need my own Ethereum node?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.node.a: No. Your validator checks every answer from any Ethereum server against Ethereum’s block headers, with its own light client. A server can be slow, but it can’t make your validator sign a wrong result.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.eth.q: Do I need ETH, or to stake anything?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.eth.a: No. Nothing is staked at any tier. The Great tier runs an Ethereum node, not an Ethereum validator.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.intern: How much of my internet will it use?
About {wire} a month from the default servers. That fits almost any home plan. It matters only on a metered or satellite link.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.addres: Will other people see my home address?
Not with the defaults. At home the validator only connects out, opens no port, and sends everything through its built-in Tor client, Ethereum calls included.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.pi.q: Can I use a Raspberry Pi?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.pi.a: Yes. {ram} of memory is best; a {min} Pi runs it with little room to spare. Use the {os}, and boot from an SSD rather than an SD card.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.os.q: Can I run it on a Mac or a Windows PC?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.os.a: Yes: {mac}, or {windows}. Windows on Arm is not supported. Turn off sleep while it runs; the commands are under {link}.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.wifi.q: Is Wi-Fi fine, or do I need a cable?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.wifi.a: Wi-Fi works. A cable drops less often, which is why the Good tier asks for one.
Which cloud provider should I pick?
Any of them works, and Arm types cost less at AWS and Azure. If you run more than one machine, put each at a different provider; {link} say why. A machine at home or at work helps the network more.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.oracle: For the test phase, yes: {free}, free. Since {halved} it is half its old size, and Oracle may reclaim an idle free instance; a validator looks idle by its measures. For a validator meant to stay up, upgrade the account to pay-as-you-go. There {paygSize} cost {payg} a month: Oracle’s price list and its Always Free page disagree on how much stays free.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.bill.q: Will my cloud bill include the Ethereum data?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.bill.a: No. Clouds charge for data going out, and almost all of a validator’s data comes in. Its own upload is {upload} a month, an estimate not yet measured.

explained.validators.hardware.hwk.home.b: Store prices read {date} at PiShop.us, Adafruit, GMKtec, Beelink, samsung.com and datacenterdisk.com. Hardware spread over {months}, power at {kwh} a kWh, the EIA’s US average.
